title: Phases, Components, and the Gibbs Rule
description: What a phase diagram is — and what it tells you

concepts.title: Phases and Components
concepts.contentHtml:
A phase is a region of matter that is uniform in composition, structure, and properties. Solid α-iron, solid γ-iron, liquid iron, and gaseous iron are four different phases of the same element.

A component is a chemically independent species. The Pb-Sn system has two components (lead and tin); the iron-carbon system has two (iron and carbon).

A phase diagram is a map showing which phases are stable at every combination of temperature, pressure, and composition. Reading one tells you what microstructure to expect when you cool an alloy slowly enough to reach equilibrium — and therefore which mechanical, electrical, and corrosion behaviour to plan for.

concepts.title: The Gibbs Phase Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
For a system at equilibrium, the number of independent intensive variables you can change while staying in the same set of phases is given by the Gibbs phase rule:

F = C − P + 2

where F is the number of degrees of freedom, C is the number of components, and P is the number of phases. The 2 counts temperature and pressure.

Example: a single-component system (C = 1) with one phase (P = 1) gives F = 2 — both T and P can vary freely. Two phases coexist along a curve (F = 1). Three phases coexist only at a single point (F = 0) — the triple point. This is exactly the structure of every pressure-temperature phase diagram.

concepts.title: Pressure-Temperature Diagrams
concepts.contentHtml:
For a single substance at varying T and P, the phase diagram is a 2-D plot showing solid, liquid, and gas regions separated by phase boundaries.

  • Triple point — solid, liquid, and gas in equilibrium. For water: 273.16 K, 611.7 Pa (defining the kelvin until 2019).
  • Critical point — the liquid-gas boundary terminates. Above the critical T and P, no distinction between liquid and gas exists; the substance is a supercritical fluid. For water: 647 K, 22.06 MPa.
  • Sublimation — solid converts directly to gas (CO₂ at 1 atm has no liquid phase, hence 'dry ice').

Many materials have surprisingly rich phase diagrams. Pure iron alone has α (BCC), γ (FCC), δ (BCC), and ε (HCP) phases under different P-T conditions, plus the liquid and gas phases.

title: Binary Eutectic Systems
description: Solder, solidus, liquidus, and the eutectic point

concepts.title: The Eutectic Diagram
concepts.contentHtml:
A binary eutectic diagram (constant pressure, two components) plots temperature vs composition. Two key lines:

  • Liquidus — above this temperature everything is liquid.
  • Solidus — below this everything is solid.

Between them lies a two-phase mush of solid + liquid. The two liquidus lines meet at the eutectic point, the lowest-temperature liquid in the system. At that exact composition, the alloy melts and freezes at a single temperature — there is no mush.

The classical example is lead-tin solder: pure Pb melts at 327 °C, pure Sn at 232 °C, but the eutectic composition (~62 % Sn) melts at 183 °C — a useful soldering temperature low enough not to damage components.

concepts.title: Microstructures of Eutectic Alloys
concepts.contentHtml:
How the alloy solidifies depends on its starting composition relative to the eutectic point:

  • Hypoeutectic (less than the eutectic composition) — primary solid α grains form first; the remaining liquid eventually reaches the eutectic point and solidifies as a fine α + β eutectic mixture between the α grains.
  • Eutectic (exactly the eutectic composition) — the entire melt freezes as a fine, characteristic lamellar α + β structure.
  • Hypereutectic — same as hypoeutectic but with primary β grains.

The lamellar eutectic forms because the two phases need to share atoms across short distances; fine alternating layers minimise diffusion distance during solidification. This is why eutectic alloys often have characteristic, easily recognisable microstructures under the microscope.

concepts.title: Why Solder Switched to Tin-Silver-Copper
concepts.contentHtml:
Tin-lead solder has an unbeatable melting behaviour — sharp eutectic at 183 °C, eutectic microstructure that solidifies smoothly. But lead is a neurotoxin. The European Union's Restriction of Hazardous Substances (RoHS) directive (2006) banned lead in most consumer electronics.

The replacement, SAC305 (96.5 % Sn, 3 % Ag, 0.5 % Cu), is a near-eutectic ternary alloy melting around 217 °C. The higher temperature stresses heat-sensitive components, the joints are more brittle, and tin whiskers are a known reliability hazard. Designing reliable lead-free solder joints required reformulating reflow profiles, board materials, and component packaging — a decade of materials engineering driven by a single phase-diagram constraint.

title: The Lever Rule and Tie Lines
description: Reading exact phase fractions off a phase diagram

concepts.title: Tie Lines
concepts.contentHtml:
Inside a two-phase region, a horizontal line at the temperature of interest — the tie line — terminates on the boundaries of the two phases. The tie-line endpoints give the compositions of the two coexisting phases at that temperature, regardless of the overall alloy composition.

For example, in a Pb-Sn system at 200 °C inside the (α + L) region, one end of the tie line gives the Sn content of the α-Pb solid solution at 200 °C; the other end gives the Sn content of the liquid that coexists with it. Both values are read straight off the diagram.

concepts.title: The Lever Rule
concepts.contentHtml:
To find the amounts of each phase, apply the lever rule on the tie line:

fraction of phase α = (length of tie line on the β side) / (total tie line)

The overall composition is the fulcrum; the further you sit from a phase, the less of that phase you have. This is exactly a mass balance: the alloy's composition must equal the weighted average of the two phase compositions.

The lever rule turns a phase diagram from a qualitative map into a quantitative tool. With a temperature, an overall composition, and the diagram, you can predict the exact mass fraction of every phase present at equilibrium.
mathExpressions: f_\alpha = \frac{C_\beta - C_0}{C_\beta - C_\alpha}, \quad f_\beta = \frac{C_0 - C_\alpha}{C_\beta - C_\alpha}

concepts.title: From Diagrams to Real Microstructures
concepts.contentHtml:
Phase diagrams describe equilibrium — the state reached after infinite time. Real cooling rarely waits that long. The actual microstructure depends on:

  • Cooling rate — slow cooling traces the equilibrium path; fast cooling can suppress phase transformations entirely (martensite in steel, glass in polymers).
  • Diffusion distances — when atoms cannot move far enough to homogenise, individual grains develop composition gradients (coring).
  • Nucleation barriers — phases predicted by the diagram may form much later than expected, or not at all, if nucleation is slow.

The diagram is the road map; kinetics tells you whether the alloy actually drives down it or takes a shortcut to a metastable structure. The most powerful materials engineering deliberately exploits non-equilibrium states the diagram does not show.

title: The Iron-Carbon Diagram
description: Steel, cementite, austenite, ferrite — the most studied phase diagram on Earth

concepts.title: Phases of the Fe-C System
concepts.contentHtml:
The Fe-C phase diagram (more precisely the Fe-Fe₃C diagram for industrial steels) is the foundation of all metallurgy. The key phases:

  • α-Ferrite — BCC iron with low carbon solubility (0.022 % max at 727 °C). Soft, ductile, magnetic.
  • γ-Austenite — FCC iron with much higher carbon solubility (~2.1 % max at 1147 °C). Soft, non-magnetic; the high-temperature parent phase.
  • δ-Ferrite — BCC iron at very high temperatures, present only above 1394 °C.
  • Cementite (Fe₃C) — hard, brittle iron carbide containing 6.67 % C by mass.
  • Liquid iron — above the liquidus.

Carbon content classification: steel < 2.1 % C, cast iron 2.1–6.67 % C. Both ranges are defined by the diagram's solubility limits.

concepts.title: Eutectoid Pearlite
concepts.contentHtml:
The most studied feature of the Fe-C diagram is the eutectoid point at 727 °C and 0.76 % C, where austenite (γ) decomposes into a fine lamellar mixture of ferrite (α) and cementite (Fe₃C):

γ (0.76 % C) → α (0.02 % C) + Fe₃C (6.67 % C)

The product is called pearlite because the alternating layers diffract light into mother-of-pearl colours under a microscope. A 0.76 % C steel slowly cooled from above 727 °C is almost entirely pearlite — strong, hard, but still reasonably ductile.

Hypoeutectoid steels (< 0.76 % C) are softer mixtures of free ferrite + pearlite. Hypereutectoid steels (> 0.76 % C) contain free cementite + pearlite, increasing hardness but reducing ductility.

concepts.title: Quenching and Martensite
concepts.contentHtml:
If austenite is cooled fast enough that carbon does not have time to diffuse out, the FCC lattice cannot transform to equilibrium BCC. Instead it shears into a strained body-centred tetragonal (BCT) structure called martensite.

Martensite is hard and brittle. It is not on the equilibrium phase diagram — it is a metastable product of the diffusionless shear transformation. Modern steel heat treatment exploits martensite extensively:

  1. Heat the steel into the austenite region (typically ~850 °C).
  2. Quench rapidly (water or oil) to lock in martensite.
  3. Temper by reheating to 200–600 °C, allowing controlled cementite precipitation and recovering ductility.

This sequence — quench and temper — is how every kitchen knife, screwdriver tip, gear, and bearing acquires its working hardness. The phase diagram alone does not predict martensite, but it underpins the heat-treatment recipe that produces it.

title: Solid Solutions and Solubility
description: Hume-Rothery rules, intermetallic compounds, and ordered phases

concepts.title: Hume-Rothery Rules
concepts.contentHtml:
For two metals to form an extensive substitutional solid solution, William Hume-Rothery showed in the 1920s that four conditions are favourable:

  1. Atomic radii within ~15 % of each other.
  2. Same crystal structure in the pure metals.
  3. Similar electronegativity.
  4. Same valence.

Examples: Cu-Ni — both FCC, similar size, similar electronegativity, similar valence (+1 to +2). They form a complete solid solution at all compositions.

Cu-Zn (brass) — similar size and electronegativity but Zn is HCP. Solubility of Zn in Cu reaches ~38 % before a second phase (β-brass) appears. Reverse: Cu in Zn is much smaller because the rules are not all satisfied.

concepts.title: Intermetallic Compounds
concepts.contentHtml:
When two metals violate Hume-Rothery rules badly enough — large size mismatch, very different electronegativities — they instead form intermetallic compounds: phases with a fixed stoichiometry and a unique crystal structure, often more like a chemical compound than an alloy.

Examples:

  • Ni₃Al (γ' phase) — the strengthening precipitate in nickel-base superalloys for jet engines.
  • Fe₃C (cementite) — the hard phase in steels.
  • NiTi — the basis of nitinol shape-memory alloys.
  • Mg₂Si — strengthens cast aluminium alloys.
  • TiAl — used in lightweight high-temperature aerospace components.

Intermetallics often combine high stiffness, high melting point, and surprising chemistry — but typically also brittleness, which is the main barrier to their wider use.

concepts.title: Order-Disorder Transitions and Modern Frontiers
concepts.contentHtml:
Solid solutions can be disordered (atoms randomly distributed across lattice sites) or ordered (specific sites occupied by specific species). Cu-Au at 50/50 composition forms an ordered superlattice (CuAu type) below ~390 °C; above it, the same alloy is randomly disordered. The transition has measurable consequences for diffraction, electrical resistivity, and mechanical hardening.

A modern frontier is the family of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) — alloys with five or more principal components in roughly equal proportions, like CrMnFeCoNi. Their configurational entropy is so high that the disordered solid solution remains stable instead of decomposing into intermetallics. HEAs offer surprising combinations of strength and ductility down to cryogenic temperatures, and challenge the binary-diagram-centric tradition of metallurgy.
